Computable Analysis / Infinite series

GEOMETRY → RATIONAL CURVE → SERIES

Leibniz’s geometric quadrature

A circle becomes an area under a rational curve. Quadrature of powers then gives the alternating series for π.

This is a modern finite reconstruction of Leibniz’s transmutation method. His early moment argument and his later general transmutation argument are related but distinct; we formalize the latter’s geometric idea. Horváth’s historical account, especially pp. 78–81, explains this distinction.

1. Read the circle through its tangent

Translate the unit circle so its centre is (1,0). On its upper-left quadrant, write

X(t) = 2t²/(1+t²),   Y(t) = 2t/(1+t²),   0 ≤ t ≤ 1.

These rational coordinates satisfy (X − 1)² + Y² = 1. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius. Its vertical intercept is t, because Y(t)t = X(t). At t = 0 the tangent is vertical; the endpoint identity does not imply a unique intercept.

2. Transmute the area, then take its complement

A trapezoid splits into an endpoint rectangle difference and a triangle measured by the line’s intercept. Summing over a finite chain cancels the intermediate rectangles. Interchanging horizontal and vertical coordinates accounts for the complementary area.

2 ∫ y dx = xy + ∫ t dx,    ∫ t dx + ∫ x dt = xt.

At the circle’s endpoint (1,1), these identities identify the quarter-circle area with the complement of half the area J under the transformed curve:

A(1) = 1 − J/2,    J = ∫₀¹ 2t²/(1+t²) dt.

The integral signs here describe certified rational area computations. The formal proof replaces infinitesimals by an exact finite correction.

3. Keep the finite error visible

For any rational cell [p,r], let T be the trapezoid under X. The existing geometric sector lower increment satisfies

sectorLower(p,r) = (r − p) − T/2 − E(p,r),
E(p,r) = (r − p)³ / [2(1+p²)(1+r²)].

On the mesh with 2ⁿ equal cells, this sums to an exact identity, with a shrinking error:

polygonLower(n) = 1 − ½ ΣT − ΣE,
0 ≤ ΣE ≤ ½ · 4⁻ⁿ.

This is proved for every n. Endpoint rectangles also bracket every geometric increment, giving the new overlap proof. The transformed integral is a valid RealRaw computation with interval width at most 8/(n+1).

4. Quadrature the powers

Finite geometric division expands the rational curve into powers with a signed remainder. Integrating each power gives

J = 2(⅓ − ⅕ + ⅐ − ⋯),
A(1) = 1 − ⅓ + ⅕ − ⅐ + ⋯,
π = 4A(1) = 4(1 − ⅓ + ⅕ − ⅐ + ⋯).

The power quadrature reuses our existing polynomial FTC results through 1 − X(t)/2 = 1/(1+t²). The geometric transmutation proof itself uses finite rational areas. The original geometric π is retained.

The checked theorem

  piCircleArea.Equiv leibnizRaw
